extracted.intended_audience: research funders, program officers, grant applicants, and research reform advocates interested in metascience and funding reform
extracted.subtask_description: Implicit rubric for what funders should value when evaluating research grants from a metascience/reform perspective: emphasizes reproducibility, openness, adequate power, genuine innovation, diversity, and mechanisms to de-risk bold ideas. Applies to designing review criteria and to applicants writing reform-minded proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducible research
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding should reward reproducible research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether study procedures, analyses, and outputs are described and packaged so independent teams can reproduce results; prefer designs and deliverables that make reproduction feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for replication studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Replication studies are systematically underfunded and should be prioritized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate dedicated funds for direct and conceptual replications; treat replication as a legitimate deliverable rather than a lower-status activity. Reviewers should value proposals that plan replication work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-registered analysis plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-registration should be standard: include a pre-registered analysis plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require or strongly encourage pre-registration of hypotheses, primary/secondary outcomes, and analysis pipelines; use pre-registration to limit post-hoc flexibility and p-hacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open data, code, and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Open data and code should be the default commitment for funded research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require explicit plans for sharing data, code, and materials (with handling for privacy/ethics); penalize proposals that keep data/code closed. Include timelines and repositories for sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing negative and null results
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative results have value and should be acknowledged and rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should not penalize null outcomes; consider incentives or dedicated publication/recognition mechanisms for well-run studies that produce negative findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-risk / high-reward funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders should enable real risk-taking when the funder asks for it rather than defaulting to incremental projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design funding streams and review processes to accept higher failure rates for potentially transformative projects; evaluate willingness to accept plausible risk and uncertainty in proposed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to reduce reviewer risk aversion (e.g., lotteries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative mechanisms (lotteries, etc.) can address systemic risk aversion in review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider partial-randomization or lottery elements for high-risk funding pools, or other process changes that reduce incentives for conservative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine innovation (not incrementalism dressed as innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of 'innovation' must be substantiated; reviewers should distinguish true novelty from marginal, safe extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear articulation of how the project would change knowledge/practice; scrutinize whether 'innovation' is real or rhetorical. Beware of bibliometric cues that mask conservatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding bibliometric overreliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric assessment perpetuates conservatism and should not be the dominant selection criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative evaluation of contribution and rigor rather than relying heavily on citation counts, journal venue, or simplistic metrics that favor established directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralizing funding (reduce concentration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of funding concentration: top institutions and PIs receive disproportionate funding and productivity per dollar declines with concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider policies that limit excessive concentration, spread resources to productive mid-tier investigators, and measure productivity per dollar when designing portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting new investigator pipelines
rubrics_metrics.description: New investigator pipelines need explicit protection and support from funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create funding streams, review criteria, or quotas that favor early-career investigators; avoid resubmission churn and structural barriers that disadvantage newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and demographic diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders should value geographic and demographic diversity among grantees and study cohorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include diversity of investigators and participant cohorts as an assessment dimension; require plans to recruit diverse populations and to assess generalizability across settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate sample sizes and power
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate power for realistic effect sizes is necessary; proposals should include power calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require power analyses using conservative, plausible effect-size estimates; penalize underpowered designs that increase false positives or exaggerated effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicable methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology must be designed to be replicable rather than just novel-seeming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether methods are described and standardized enough to be replicated; prefer pre-specified analytic workflows and standard operating procedures when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest acknowledgment of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should honestly acknowledge uncertainty and avoid overstating confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the realism of effect-size estimates, error bars, and limitations sections; favor conservative interpretations and transparent discussion of potential failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear contribution to knowledge over publication count
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding decisions should prioritize clear contributions to knowledge, not raw publication or citation counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask applicants to make explicit what knowledge will change and how; evaluate substance of contribution rather than volume metrics or 'citation-chasing' behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Built-in plans for replication and independent replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Good proposals include plans for replication or built-in generalizability testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require replication within the project design where appropriate, or explicit plans and incentives for independent replication after initial results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage p-hacking and selective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs that enable p-hacking or selective reporting should be penalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require pre-specification of primary outcomes, analytic decision trees, and justification for subgroup analyses; evaluate analytic transparency and multiplicity controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability within collaborative structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Mega-consortia with diffuse accountability are problematic; clear accountability is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require governance plans, named responsible parties, milestones, and mechanisms for attribution and oversight in multi-site or consortium proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hype and overstated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Hype language that exceeds the evidence should be criticized and devalued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the alignment between claims and evidence; penalize promotional framing that is not supported by preliminary data or realistic plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability and multi-cohort evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-population studies should not be framed as broadly generalizable without justification; cohort diversity and broad generalizability matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require plans to test or explain limits of generalizability; prefer multi-site, multi-population designs or explicit replication across cohorts when generalization is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund replication infrastructure and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need to build and fund infrastructure that supports replication (platforms, registries, repositories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support investments in shared infrastructure (data repositories, pre-registration platforms, replication incentives) as a legitimate funding priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding funder-grantee revolving door conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Funder–grantee revolving door dynamics and conflicts of interest reduce trust and should be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement transparency and conflict-of-interest policies; evaluate institutional and reviewer independence to avoid capture or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant practices rewarded by reform-minded reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific applicant behaviors that increase chances: pre-register analysis, state open science commitments, use conservative power calculations, recruit diverse cohorts, acknowledge limitations, cite replication work, avoid hype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should include explicit pre-registration links, data/code sharing plans, conservative effect-size and power justifications, a priori subgroup and outcome specifications, and plain-language limitations. These are actionable signals reviewers will value.
